summary: On Tuesday, October 17, 2023, the City Council passed a package of public safety measures for the downtown district, including high-definition CCTV cameras, more police officers, and expanded community crime-prevention programs. The roughly $4.5 million plan is funded by general fund reallocations, public safety grants, and a modest local sales tax increase. Police largely welcomed it, while civil liberties groups, some small business owners, and some residents raised concerns about over-policing and prices. The Council promised training in de-escalation and cultural sensitivity, task forces, and quarterly reviews.
one_line: The City Council approved a $4.5 million downtown public safety package of cameras, more police, and community programs, drawing both support and criticism.
key_facts: The City Council passed the downtown public safety measures on Tuesday, October 17, 2023, at a meeting with unusually high turnout.
The measures total an estimated $4.5 million, funded by reallocations from the city's general fund, public safety grants, and a modest local sales tax increase.
The plan funds high-definition CCTV cameras throughout downtown, with strategic placement in known trouble spots.
Police Chief Eduardo Velasquez advocated hiring additional officers to patrol downtown, particularly during evening hours.
Neighborhood watch groups and community policing initiatives are earmarked for expansion.

Mayor Jacqueline Mendoza leads the Council; Councilman James Peterson, chair of the Finance Committee, confirmed the plan has a sizable price tag but called it an investment in the community's future.
Councilmember Liu Wong said, "People don't feel safe walking the streets after dark."
Captain Andrea Ruiz, officer in charge of downtown policing, said "We are stretched thin" and welcomed more personnel.
The Downtown Civil Rights Coalition argues increased surveillance and policing might infringe individual freedoms and disproportionately affect marginalized communities.
Lia Chen, owner of 'Downtown Deli,' worries the higher sales tax will make customers shy away due to higher prices.
Resident Alejandra Ramirez, a college student, is wary of heavy-handed policing and wants assurance of accountability and proper training.
The Council plans training programs on de-escalation techniques, cultural sensitivity, and community relationship building for officers.
The Council committed to quarterly reviews of the impact on crime rates, community relations, and economic health.
Task forces of community leaders, Council members, and law enforcement representatives will work on implementation details in the coming weeks.
